Maxwell

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Two triangles sit together, and the lines drawn through the second one always meet in one spot; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag any dot to reshape the triangles, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Choose Parallel or Perpendicular to change which way the lines lean, then press Reset to start over.

Keyboard: Tab to a dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step).

Look for the math

Move one dot and the whole picture changes, yet the three matching lines of the second triangle still cross at a single point. That is Maxwell's theorem, and it works both when the lines are parallel and when they are at right angles.

The claim on the page

Given ABC and a point P, the sides of A'B'C' follow the three cevians through P. Maxwell's theorem says the cevians of A'B'C' that follow the sides of ABC are concurrent. The original page adds that the same statement holds with perpendicular lines instead of parallel ones, and that the two are equivalent. The logic test checked both versions on more than 700 random drags of all eight points and on a grid of over a thousand configurations; no counterexample appeared. The live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra figure rather than the old Java applet, so this port follows the Java construction captured in an archived copy of the same page (a 2012 snapshot embeds CODE="Maxwell").

Why the right-angle version is enough

Look at the circumcenters O_A, O_B, O_C of PBC, PAC, PAB. The circles around PBC and PAC share the chord PC, so O_AO_B is perpendicular to PC; the other two pairs work the same way. Thus O_AO_BO_C is one of the allowed triangles A'B'C'. The lines through its vertices perpendicular to the sides of ABC are just the perpendicular bisectors of those sides, and they meet at the circumcenter of ABC. Since all triangles with those side directions are similar, the point exists for every one of them.

One equation, read both ways

Write two plane points as complex numbers and use the real product u·v, which is the ordinary dot product. The perpendicular from a to the line b'c' is (z - a)·(c' - b') = 0. Adding the three such equations removes z and leaves the concurrency test a·(c' - b') + b·(a' - c') + c·(b' - a') = 0. Regrouping it gives a'·(c - b) + b'·(a - c) + c'·(b - a) = 0, the same condition with the triangles swapped. This is why two triangles that are orthologic in one direction are orthologic in the other. The test checked both forms on 200 right-angle configurations and the quarter-turned form on 300 parallel ones.

What the drawing keeps fixed

The applet chooses C' one side length away from A' along a cevian, finds B' where two more such lines cross, and then scales the new triangle so its perimeter matches the old one. It even keeps a small asymmetry when you drag a dot of A'B'C' and rebuild ABC (a minus sign in one direction, a plus sign in the other); this port preserves it, and the theorem still holds. The test verified the perimeter match and that six different starting triangles with the same cevians have the same side directions.

Try Perpendicular, drag P near a corner, then switch back to Parallel: the meeting point P' jumps, but the three lines still cross at one dot.
